This study investigates public expectations towards CDR across the ESG dimensions compared to other societal actors, and examines how individuals’ environmental and social consciousness, digital competence, and corporate trust shape these expectations. Drawing on a pre-registered survey of a representative sample of Dutch citizens (n = 2196) we develop and validate a measurement scale capturing ESG-related CDR expectations. Results show that citizens consistently attribute digital responsibility to companies across all ESG domains. Environmental and social consciousness, and digital competence significantly predict CDR expectations, positioning CDR as a socially constructed expectations system shaped by moral orientations and technological literacy. Corporate trust moderates these relationships: it amplifies value-based expectations while reducing competence-driven demands. Our findings advance CDR scholarship beyond technical, managerial, and conceptual accounts by empirically grounding CDR in citizens’ responsibility attributions and situating it within broader debates of digital governance and accountability. Our study highlights key implications of CDR communication: aligning corporate practices with public expectations is central to negotiating accountability and shaping responsible digital governance.

latest.title: Militant platform democracy: a framework for democracy-worthy platform policies
Did you make this for me? A two-country study on individuals’ perceptions of tailoring in online political ads
latest.abstract: Online targeted advertising has seen increasing use by political actors. With this technique, messages can be tailored to align with the preferences of individual recipients. In this study, we address the lack of understanding about the factors that influence voters' perceptions of political ads as tailored, as well as the extent to which tailoring perceptions (e.g., the extent to which an individual experiences a message as fitting to them) influence ad evaluation. We first argue that the issue content and the sending parties are the main drivers behind the perception of a political ad as tailored. Subsequently, we hypothesize that perceived tailoring influences ad evaluation positively. Lastly, we test what drives tailoring effects: actual tailoring or perceptions of it. To test these hypotheses, we employ an innovative design to capture ad exposure and responses. We combine the mobile experience sampling method (mESM) with data donations in the form of screenshots of actual ads received by respondents during election campaigns in the United States (2022) and Germany (2021). Our findings confirm that partisan alignment enhances the perception of the ad as tailored. We have mixed results for the effect of issue alignment, which only increases tailoring perceptions in Germany. Furthermore, ads perceived as tailored are evaluated more positively in both the US and Germany. Lastly, we find evidence for partial mediation through tailoring perceptions. Our findings have important implications for understanding the mechanisms of how targeted political ads on social media could impact society.

latest.title: Replatformization and the expansion of the alt-tech ecosystem on kiwi farms
latest.abstract: This paper develops ‘replatformization’ to evaluate the re-constitutive practices of alternative platforms. Alt-tech platforms that cater to ‘deplatformed’ reactionary users characterize themselves as unregulated, obfuscating how they adopt governance tactics to subvert deplatformization. Through a case study of the harassment forum Kiwi Farms, I characterize replatformization as a strategy by which alternative platforms build a ‘stack-to-come’ which exercises control of digital infrastructure within an existent regulatory model. I analyze Kiwi Farms’ replatformization between 2013 and 2025, focusing on its social, technical, and organizational tactics to evade corporate deplatforming under market-based governance. This paper elucidates three general characteristics of replatformization. First, replatformization is a sociotechnical process which requires not only technical administration but also the consolidation of capital and labor, persuasive campaigning, and proliferation of organizational apparatuses to sustain independent infrastructure. Second, replatformization intensifies the foundational values of an imperiled platform, which, for alt-tech platforms, entails a deeper descent into reactionary vitriol. Third, replatformization efforts scale after each instance of deplatforming, reflecting the ecological character of the platform economy. Alt-tech replatformization aligns with the market-based model of governance while posturing as an alternative to it, obscuring more democratic possibilities for platform governance. The three tenants of replatformization offer researchers a heuristic with which to investigate how any alternative platform, not just alt-tech, positions itself as ‘alternative’ to a platform ecosystem.

latest.title: The echoes from social media: modeling how filter bubbles and network structure shape echo chamber emergence
latest.abstract: The extent of echo chambers in social media and their impact on polarization is an open debate in the political science literature. There is mixed evidence about the extent to which these opinion-reinforcement communities exist and contribute to polarization and the erosion of social cohesion. This paper employs a social simulation approach that draws on political communication and social influence theories to explain how echo chambers can emerge on social media platforms. The agent-based model developed here integrates individual social networks (online and offline) with opinion dynamics to untangle the respective roles of social media algorithms and social network structures. Simulation conditions separately manipulated (1) the homophily or group similarity in personal networks and (2) the level of selective exposure to confirming information through filter bubbles on social media. We found that individuals’ information exposure significantly influenced echo chamber emergence, particularly in initially random social networks where people are surrounded by a diverse group of others. At the same time, artificially creating echo chambers did not ensure their persistence over time in the presence of filtering algorithms. Overall, we need to reconsider how we understand echo chambers and the mechanisms responsible for this phenomenon.

latest.title: Everyday feminist tagging as techno-rhetorical strategy: interference and curation through Instagram hashtags in #Kvinnostrejk
latest.abstract: Hashtag use in online protest is widespread and well-researched. Yet scholarship has largely focused on viral moments and large-scale mobilisations, leaving everyday, platform-native, and sustained practices comparatively underexamined. These routine forms of tagging can subtly intervene in the engagement-driven sorting logics that shape visibility online and contribute to gradual forms of consciousness-raising among unexpected audiences. This study explores everyday use of hashtags through the Swedish feminist initiative #Kvinnostrejk (women’s strike), mobilised continuously since 2021. It examines how routine tagging practices push feminist content into otherwise unrelated streams, assemble newsfeeds into collective narratives of gendered violence, and carry tags across online and offline contexts as recognisable political symbols. By introducing the concept of techno-rhetorical strategies, the article contributes in two ways: it shows how small-scale tagging practices shape visibility without relying on virality, and it extends sociotechnical perspectives that emphasise the role of platform-specific affordances by foregrounding the inseparability of technical operations and rhetorical effects.

latest.title: An exploration of smart speakers to support independence, competence, and relatedness for older adults at risk of digital exclusion in public and social housing
latest.abstract: This was mixed-methods longitudinal study where ninety-eight participants were randomly assigned to receive a smart speaker immediately (intervention group) or after three months (wait-list control). Wellbeing (ONS4) and loneliness (De Jong Gierveld Loneliness Scale) were measured at baseline, three, and nine months, alongside in-depth qualitative interviews. Voice-recordings from the devices were also collected. Participants primarily used smart speakers for entertainment, information, and reminders, reporting benefits associated with autonomy (convenient control of routines, access to entertainment), competence (confidence and cognitive stimulation, health behaviours), and relatedness (device-based companionship). However, no significant changes were found in quantitative measures of wellbeing or loneliness. Barriers included technology apprehension, low self-efficacy, and accessibility challenges, while facilitators included gradual learning, peer support, and supportive staff. Findings suggest that smart speakers support technologically mediated companionship, which is not captured well by standard interpersonal measures of loneliness. Furthermore, smart speaker engagement creates bidirectional feedback loops, where use fosters confidence and perceived autonomy, which in turn promotes further use. Our findings from a social housing population are consistent with broader socio-technical perspectives, where digital inclusion is relational and context-dependent, requiring social scaffolding and organisational support.

latest.title: Privacy and power in the smart home: housing market conditions and exposure to smart devices in home environments
latest.abstract: The diffusion of smart home technology is often studied through a lens of adoption, where preferences, attitudes, and inequalities in access and use are a key concern. In this article, we shift to a framework of exposure to smart home devices – which encompasses both proactive adoption and involuntary (or even undesired) exposure. We also distinguish between property-based smart devices that belong to homes and individual-based devices that belong to persons. Using data from a nationally representative survey of adults in the United States, we examine the role of household characteristics and housing market conditions in organizing exposure. We find that renters’ exposure to property-based smart devices is more responsive to new housing construction than homeowners’ exposure. We also find that Black exposure to property-based smart devices increases relative to white exposure as the level of Black–white segregation increases. Broadly, our findings highlight how individual exposure to smart devices is shaped by broader housing market dynamics, household conditions, and social inequalities that stem from structural conditions of power and inequality rather than individual preferences or attitudes about specific benefits or risks of technology.

latest.title: The missing ontology: why platform interventions systematically fail
latest.abstract: This paper examines a profound philosophical disjunction in platform capitalism: corporate actors, despite their technological orientation, operate as practical realists through sophisticated mechanism design and multi-layered interventions, while critical scholars and reformers, despite their social science foundations, remain trapped in an instrumental-technological view of platforms. Applying relational emergence theory from critical realist philosophy, we demonstrate how digital platforms function as emergent entities whose causal powers and properties transcend their constituent technological components. Through analysis of worker reclassification efforts and platform cooperativism initiatives, we reveal how this ontological asymmetry produces persistent reform failures: platform organizations continuously redesign mechanisms to preserve essential extractive properties, effectively neutralizing reformers’ surface-level interventions through strategic reorganization of underlying mechanisms. Our philosophical analysis challenges the dominant conception of platforms as neutral technological tools that can be simply reformed or repurposed, revealing them instead as emergent entities purposefully designed for value extraction. This perspective makes three key contributions: (1) developing a comprehensive emergent ontology of platforms that bridges technological and social dimensions; (2) providing an ontologically-grounded explanation for the recurring failure of reform efforts – what we term platform morphostasis; and (3) proposing new conceptual foundations for effective resistance based on engaging with platforms at the level of their generative mechanisms rather than their empirical consequences. The paper ultimately argues that addressing platform dominance requires critical actors to adopt the realist ontological approach that has proven so effective for corporate platform developers.

latest.title: Media effects, selection effects, or no effects? A longitudinal analysis of the relationship between media use and misperceptions
Platforming pocket money: family finance apps and the datafication of child economies
latest.abstract: Family finance apps are digital platforms that offer possibilities for reshaping children’s consumer socialization and economic agency. These finance apps incorporate functions for both parents and children through the setting and tracking of chores, the payment of allowances or pocket money, as well as the monitoring and management of children’s saving and spending. With these apps, children’s economic experiences and participation are increasingly platformed and datafied. That is, guided by functionality for data tracking and analysis. This paper offers a study of the datafication dimensions of these apps as a basis for further research in the emerging area of children’s fintech. The paper undertakes an analysis of features across popular child finance apps, exploring their role in the datafication of children’s financial and economic participation. This discussion is contextualized in relation to child finance and digital platform literature to understand how these apps mediate and craft children as financial subjects via affordances that provide regular allowance or pocket money payments and increased purchasing power. In turn, we consider how they construct children as financial objects through financial data management and monitoring by parents, platforms, and the financial industry. We argue that the data produced by child finance apps simultaneously enables and exploits children’s economic lives, initiating conditions for and expectations of lifelong digital finance tracking.

latest.title: Disability and AI in smart cities: centering access, agency, and awareness in hybrid spaces
Socioeconomic and digital divides in public support for AI-driven welfare decisions: cross-national evidence from 21 countries
latest.abstract: As governments increasingly deploy artificial intelligence (AI) for automated decision-making, little is known about why citizens differ in their attitudes toward AI-driven decision-making in the public sector, especially in welfare governance, where decisions carry profound consequences for marginalized groups. As prior scholarship suggests that automated systems can act as a digital poorhouse that punishes low-income individuals, this paper examines whether there exists a socioeconomic divergence in public opinion and how a digital divide perspective helps explain this divergence across countries. Through a cross-national survey, the study finds that individuals experiencing economic hardship and holding negative attitude toward AI express significantly less support for AI-driven welfare decisions than their counterparts. The study further shows that the country-level divide in Human Development Index and internet penetration can further condition the effects of economic hardship and general AI attitude on support for AI-driven welfare decisions. Overall, the study not only highlights the importance of addressing the inequalities embedded in the politics of automation but also calls for future research to examine the role of the digital divide in shaping public opinion across policy domains and societal contexts.

latest.title: Measuring partisan community dynamics: a longitudinal analysis of affective engagement in pro-Bolsonaro Facebook networks
latest.abstract: This study examines how major political events shape affective engagement patterns in a hyperpartisan pro-Bolsonaro network of Facebook accounts. Hyperpartisan communities are often characterized as impermeable echo chambers with predictable engagement patterns, yet this assumption has rarely been tested longitudinally. Using a mixed-methods approach combining LLM-based content classification, time series analysis, and regression modeling, we analyze over 12 million posts from 53 Brazilian pro-Bolsonaro groups and pages across 2021–2023. Two behavioral indices were constructed: the Emotional Polarization Index measuring love-versus-angry reactions, and the Engagement Balance Index capturing comment-versus-share interactions. Results show that hyperpartisan communities displayed surprisingly unstable engagement patterns over time, contradicting traditional theories that assume polarization as consistent. A major shift occurred in 2023 around Lula's inauguration and the January coup attempt, marked by declining emotional intensity, increased internal debate, and weakening opposition responses. These findings suggest that engagement dynamics extend beyond fixed ideological positions, shaped by major political events and contextual changes. The study contributes methodologically through its longitudinal approach and use of machine learning for political actor recognition, offering new insights into the dynamic nature of digital political polarization.

latest.title: Typology of transparency as best practice: evidence from facial recognition technologies in Australia
latest.abstract: Facial recognition technologies (FRTs) are commonly used in Australia in an under-regulated environment. Only two regulatory mechanisms currently direct FRT use – industry self-regulation and Australia’s privacy laws. Currently, best practices for FRT development and adoption are a key governance mechanism, including the recent guide to FRT privacy risks evaluation published by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner in 2024. Transparency is lauded as one of the key principles for implementation, yet it can be an elusive best practice to operationalize. Transparency spans everything from technical design decisions and data governance to real-world applications, user communication, and regulatory compliance. Thus, our research critically considers the concept of transparency in FRT governance by asking: What does transparency as best practice mean in the development and implementation of facial recognition systems? This study sought to map multi-stakeholder viewpoints through problem-centered interviews (n = 30) with expert technical, policy, and academic stakeholders making and informing FRT policy in Australia. Based on their responses, we develop a typology of what transparency means in the context of operationalizing algorithmic surveillance technology governance, specifically FRTs. Our findings adopt a socio-technical perspective and identify five distinct modes of transparency in FRTs, including technical, functional, procedural, public and contextual transparency.

latest.title: Linking names with frames: the interplay of moral entities and moral frames in Chinese online gender debates
latest.abstract: This study examines how moral-entity expansion in online gender debates is associated with the adoption of moral frames. Using a large-scale analysis of comments from three major gender-based violence incidents in China, we explore how different referential terms construct moral entities and relate to moral evaluations. Employing word embedding analysis, we quantified the semantic proximity between referential terms and moral axes. The results show that gender-specific terms align more closely with moral foundations, suggesting a broader, more polarised moral orientation. In contrast, gender-neutral terms primarily activate procedural evaluations, focusing on the roles of actors rather than their gender identities. This result suggests that entity expansion toward out-group members via GST broadens the scope of who is under moral consideration, while frames specify why and how that widened target should be judged, thereby leading to moralisation that is amplified in both its diversity and moral charge. This study contributes to the literature on moral expansiveness by providing discourse-level evidence of how moral boundaries are constructed. It also helps explain how the coupling of moral entities and moral frames leads to the moralisation of feminist discourse.

latest.title: Selling speed, suspending citizenship: data throttling, instantaneous downgrading, and the politics of connectivity in China
latest.abstract: This article theorizes ‘data throttling’ in China as infrastructural governance of digital citizenship via allocative control of speed. In ‘unlimited’ / ‘high-volume’ plans, connections are slowed after usage thresholds are exceeded. Based on interviews with high-data users across multiple provinces and a small corpus of social-media discourse, we find: (1) throttling is normalized through a strategically vague regime that grants operators definitional authority over ‘normal’ speed and acceptable latency; (2) throttling produces instantaneous downgrading – engineered suspensions of immediacy in payment, mobility, and work – extending speed politics to programmable latency and micro-temporal rationing; and (3) attribution of responsibility shifts from self-blame toward claims on infrastructure for minimum availability. Conceptually, we redefine digital inequality as a schedulable scarcity of usable speed. We advance the lowest speed and latency at which core civic functions remain actionable as a more precise target of governance than access per se.

latest.title: Examining initial trust development and trusting intentions toward humanoid social robots
latest.abstract: Humanoid social robots (HSRs) collect personal data and offer personalized services, fostering user reliance. Unlike passive tools, HSRs actively engage in interactions, making initial trust – formed before direct experience – critical for user acceptance. Despite its importance in reducing uncertainty and shaping first impressions, initial trust remains underexplored. To address this gap, we developed a model of initial trust formation and tested it through a study with 375 U.S. participants. The results supported five out of nine hypotheses, offering actionable insights for businesses and policymakers. Key factors such as structural assurance, perceived service benefits, and reputation play a pivotal role in cultivating early trust, thereby enhancing adoption and acceptance of HSRs.

latest.title: The politics of platformization: genealogy from administrative reform to platform governance
latest.abstract: Platform studies have been dominated by analytical and evaluative frameworks attuned to Silicon Valley techno-capitalism. This article joins a growing body of work that unsettles this universalizing orientation by reconstructing an alternative trajectory of ‘platformization’ (pingtaihua): a governing rationale and technological enactment of power rooted in Chinese public administration, later transplanted into the regulation of private platforms across China’s vast digital landscape. I map the field of platform studies through the emic–etic distinction and its underlying political and empirical stakes. Adopting an emic approach that centers historical actors’ own vocabularies and agendas, the article reconstructs a synthetic historical account with ‘platforms’ (pingtai) and ‘platformization’ (pingtaihua) as its throughline. Drawing on informatics theorist Philip Agre’s concept of ‘capture’ – a notion increasingly diluted and distorted in analyses of digital capitalism – I foreground underexamined dynamics of power in Chinese platform governance while intervening in dominant etic frameworks for understaning Silicon Valley Big Tech.

latest.title: Infrastructural hubris and platform power: the failed scalability of Google Stadia
latest.abstract: This article examines Google Stadia, a cloud gaming platform that closed in 2023 after less than four years despite being built on Google’s global infrastructure. Through a thematic analysis of 170 documents including specialized press articles, Reddit discussions, and YouTube reviews, we investigate Stadia’s failure by examining its main stakeholders’ perspectives, i.e., gamers and game developers. Drawing on infrastructure studies’ focus on breakdown and failure alongside scholarship on platform power, we introduce the concept of infrastructural hubris, i.e., the overconfidence in technical capacity that leads to neglecting platform-level engagement with key communities. We illustrate this concept via three interconnected failures of the platform. First, Stadia provided inadequate incentives for both game developers and gamers, failing to resolve the ‘chicken and egg’ problem where neither side had sufficient reason to join the platform. Second, constant strategic pivots – from full-scale gaming platform to a white-label streaming technology – undermined stakeholders’ trust over Stadia’s brief lifespan. Third, despite Google’s global infrastructure, last-mile connectivity issues and incompatible development tools limited adoption by both users and developers. The case demonstrates that infrastructural power and platform power must be studied in tandem, as technical capabilities alone cannot achieve scalability without sustained engagement at the platform level.

latest.title: The digital health capital framework: cross-cutting digital health inequality and smart-aging in post-COVID Hong Kong
latest.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has accelerated the adoption of e-health technologies while simultaneously amplifying existing digital health disparities. To identify the digital health divide, we propose the Digital Health Capital (DHC) framework, an integrated multidimensional measure including usage, literacy and transformative capacity, to scrutinize the digital health divide in the emerging technology landscape. Utilizing a mixed-mode dataset that combines a quota-sampled online survey with an offline sample of elderly participants, we apply this framework to examine the digital health capital divide in post-COVID Hong Kong. Our data reveals three findings. First, consistent with previous studies, substantial disparities in DHC scores correlated with socioeconomic status (SES): individuals with higher education, wealthier, and employment consistently exhibit stronger digital health capacities. Second, the impacts of SES on the divide vary by different dimensions of DHC, revealing that the mechanisms driving inequalities in transformative capacity differ significantly from those affecting usage and literacy. Third, the findings challenge the stereotype of the homogeneity of digital disadvantage among the elderly and highlight the overlooked disadvantage faced by the middle-aged ‘sandwiched generation.’ These findings call for more refined policies for smart aging initiatives, emphasizing the need for targeted strategies to bridge the digital health capital divide when developing techcare for diverse demographic groups.

latest.title: Weapon, wonder or both? Political framings of AI in global north and south media
latest.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly understood as a political infrastructure and a decision-making technology with the potential to reshape institutions and reconfigure power relations, media coverage plays a key role in shaping public understanding of its risks and opportunities. This study examines how mainstream media outlets in the Global North and Global South politically frame AI, emphasising the implications for digital governance and public opinion. Building on prior work that analyse AI coverage but leaves its political and emotional dimensions underexplored, the research presents a comparative analysis of 6,829 news articles (2010–2024) across twelve newspapers from Europe, North America, Africa, and Asia and Oceania, combining topic modelling and sentiment analysis. The results reveal three temporal phases: an incipient phase (2010–2016), politicisation through crises (2017–2021), and exponential acceleration (2022–2024), with salient inflection points following the Cambridge Analytica scandal (2018) and the launch of ChatGPT (2022). Fifteen thematic frames emerged, dominated by Social Media and Tech Impact (16.03 per cent), Technology and the Digital Economy (12.54 per cent), and China–US Relations and Trade (11.41 per cent). Media outlets in the North display higher levels of pessimistic coverage , with 41.7 per cent of headlines classified as negative. In contrast, media in the South express a more optimistic tone, with 51.5 per cent of headlines being positive. The study demonstrates that media narratives about AI are shaped by geopolitical disputes, differing risk perceptions, and asymmetries in technological power, stressing the need for fair, transparent and ethical AI regulation.

latest.title: From records to actions: mediating civic data and environmental activism in Taiwan
latest.abstract: This article reconceptualizes environmental data activism as situated practices that mediate actions through data infrastructures and translation. Drawing on participant observation, interviews, and document analysis of two environmental NGOs (ENGOs) in Taiwan and their collaborations with civic-tech communities, we identify three key roles of ENGOs in environmental data activism: (1) extracting and infrastructuring datasets; (2) translating and re-embedding data into everyday practices through digital tools such as mobile apps and crowdsourcing games; (3) and mediating between different social actors in data activism. Hence, we theorize ENGOs as civic data intermediaries that turn open data into civic data infrastructures. We further identify contingent civic alliances in data activism. These are volunteer-driven collaborations that are generative yet precarious, producing episodic surges of both innovation and breakdown. This article argues that the value of data emerges not from purity of measurement but from socio-technical work that renders data publicly usable and criticizable. Conceptually, the research advances a practice-based theory of data justice as infrastructural work, showing how civic groups convert data from records into connected actions in everyday activism. From this perspective, the limits of justice are set as much by the labor of maintenance, temporal rhythms, and alliance fragility as by the epistemic accuracy of data.

latest.title: ‘That’s not where the cart goes!’: ragebait as accountability entertainment
latest.abstract: Outrage is a popular way to generate attention on social media, from ragebait and trolling to callouts. Cultural producers also harness social shaming as a content production strategy, repurposing the model of activism-driven callout culture as a form of accountability entertainment, or content that both stages and spectacularizes the intervention into misbehavior. We focus on Cart Narcs, a leading cross-platform provider of accountability entertainment, examining the channel’s YouTube videos, online comments, and public interviews with the creator to identify the production strategies used to capture people in compromising situations and drive them into rage on camera. Cart Narcs is, on face, about confronting people who do not return their shopping carts, but we argue that its actual entertainment value lies instead in the way the Cart Narc expertly ragebaits people who argue with him. Ragebait appeals to content producers because it is formulaic, repeatable, and controlled, while the audience appeal instead centers around the viewer’s desire for achieving moral high ground and catharsis. Cart Narcs generates viewer enjoyment through the feeling of holding someone accountable by watching their comeuppance, but ultimately forwards a politics that is atomized, condemning individuals rather than offering a larger vision of how to incentivize prosocial behavior. Cart Narcs thus demonstrates a production formula that simultaneously claims to provide the catharsis of callouts while profiting from the induced outrage of shopping cart ne'er-do-wells.

latest.title: Balancing personalization and privacy: datafication challenges in socially assistive robotics for older persons
latest.abstract: The promise of Socially Assistive Robots (SARs) to deliver personalized care for older persons depends heavily on extensive data collection, raising concerns about privacy, autonomy, trust, and the limited involvement of older adults in shaping data-related configurations. This study examines how developers and researchers navigate the tension between personalization and privacy in the datafication process in SAR development for older people. We conducted eighteen interviews with international experts from industry and research institutes and analyzed them using a constructivist grounded theory approach. Participants identified 41 unique data types used by SARs, comprising numerous variables. In describing the datafication of older persons as SARs users, participants characterized SARs as capable of ‘collecting everything.’ Regulatory compliance and data safeguarding were framed in ‘all or nothing’ terms, leaving older adults uninvolved in personalizing or influencing data management and control over their data, effectively requiring them to accept the SAR as a whole or decline it entirely. At the same time, participants viewed control, transparency, personalization, and the storage of personal data for user identification as essential for effective social robotics. These findings reveal a personalization-data-storing paradox: privacy preserving practices and regulatory constraints often restrict data use and online connectivity, yet meaningful personalization and interaction depend on richer data use and access. We illustrate this paradox through a typology of four SAR categories and highlight the need to involve older persons in shaping meaningful data management practices that balance privacy protection with an enriched user experience.

latest.title: Driving the hype: LLMs as ‘general-purpose’ promise in the autonomous vehicle industry
latest.abstract: Proponents of autonomous vehicles are proclaiming a new era, driven by innovations derived from large language models (LLMs). Following a decade of highly public failures and the concurrent redirection of capital and attention towards generative AI, firms in the autonomous vehicle industry have turned to LLM-style techniques as the basis for a rebooted commercialisation effort. Through a technographic analysis of an annual industry event, Nvidia GTC 2024, and 41 sources of related grey literature (firm communications, technical preprints, trade journalism, and regulatory documents), we examine how two autonomous vehicle firms, Wayve and Waabi, discursively frame these techniques as capable of overcoming the technical, economic, financial, and regulatory limits that have so far thwarted a fully-autonomous future (AV 1.0). We find that these claims draw heavily on the supposed ‘general-purposivity’ of LLMs, importing assumptions about the broad applicability of foundation models, multimodal training, parallel tokenisation, and epistemic distillation (AV 2.0) into a domain where they remain largely unproven. The innovations discussed are highly speculative in nature and contribute to the discursive hype around the viability of LLM-style approaches in the autonomous vehicle industry. In promoting claims of general-purposivity, they serve as a blueprint for how proponents are seeking to embed LLMs in new industries and domains.

latest.title: The consequences of alternative media and disinformation-prone alternative media consumption on political beliefs over the course of the COVID-19 pandemic
latest.abstract: With growing distrust in mainstream media, citizens often turn to alternative sources to learn about socio-political events. There has been extensive research on how such media diets influence political attitudes and engagement. However, alternative media have served as an umbrella term for a variety of sources with various ideological leanings as well as journalistic standards. In this study, we introduce the distinction between Alternative Media (AM), which adhere more closely to journalistic standards, and Disinformation-Prone Alternative Media (DPAM), which frequently disseminate conspiratorial or misleading content. Drawing on a panel survey collected before and after COVID-19 (2019–2024) in Czechia, we examine how consumption of these two types of sources influenced political cynicism and internal political efficacy over time.Results show that DPAM consumption is significantly associated with increased political cynicism and higher internal political efficacy—suggesting that anti-establishment narratives may simultaneously erode trust in institutions while fostering a sense of political empowerment. In contrast, AM consumption was linked to a decrease in political cynicism and had no significant effect on internal efficacy. These findings challenge the assumption that all alternative media undermine democratic engagement and show the need for distinguishing between independent critical journalism and disinformation-driven sources when researching their effects on political attitudes and engagement.

latest.title: Inaccuracies, omissions, and bullshit: 2024 U.S. elections through the eyes of ChatGPT
latest.abstract: This study evaluated the accuracy, quality, and implications of outputs produced by generative artificial intelligences (AI) related to politics and electoral processes during the 2024 United States elections. We extend social media platform governance and content moderation theories to the study of AI, illustrating how large language models (LLMs), and the companies that own these technologies, shape and influence political information environments. Notably, we argue that the shift from social media to generative AI represents a fundamental evolution in platform power: a move from curative governance (providing information by sorting human speech) to generative governance (providing information by generating speech). Through a novel mixed-methods audit approach to studying ChatGPT-4o mini outputs regarding politics and elections collected less than two weeks before election day, we find that ChatGPT largely failed to provide users with accurate, reliable, and trustworthy information during a crucial election period. Our analysis identifies and categorizes potential democratic harms embedded in ChatGPT’s responses – such as inaccuracies, hedging, bullshit, and omissions – that paint a picture of a technology ill-equipped for democratic elections. This study illustrates the need for new frameworks for accountability in generative AI, particularly as voluntary industry safeguards fail to protect democratic information environments.

latest.title: Consumptive curation for self-care: in search of clumsier algorithms
latest.abstract: In this article, we explore how young adults make sense of their social media use in relation to wellbeing, focusing on their algorithmic imaginaries, practices and sense of agency. Our analysis draws on 125 data accounts collected in Austria, Estonia, Finland and the UK through interviews and autoethnographies, part of a larger research project on digital visual trust in social media communication concerning wellbeing and health. We show that young adults actively curate their social media experience by trying to interact with recommendation algorithms. They explicitly frame such curation practices as a form of self-care seeking to encourage content that supports their wellbeing and discourage content perceived as harmful. However, these practices do not always work as intended. The algorithm was perceived as reacting too quickly or slowly, sorting participants into topical silos or stubbornly ‘remembering’ past viewing behaviors. Our analysis shows that while curatorial self-care practices can be an expression of agency, this agency is partial, temporary, and shaped by the contexts in which platforms are navigated. We propose curatorial self-care as an affective, attentional, and infrastructural form of maintenance. Rather than resisting or optimizing algorithms, our participants engage in continuous negotiation with opaque algorithmic systems to adjust for more manageable digital experiences. We therefore suggest discussions around social media and wellbeing need to shift from prohibiting social media use or focusing on individual literacy and responsibility toward designing algorithms that optimize for wellbeing rather than engagement, or, as put by our participants – we need clumsier algorithms.

latest.title: Italians’ attitudes towards AI: how technology issues travel across social conversation
latest.abstract: This paper explores public perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) in Italy through the lens of science communication as a ‘social conversation around science’. Drawing on nationally representative survey data collected in 2023 and 2024 by the Observa Science in Society Monitor, it analyses how Italians access information about AI, their self-assessed information level, the use of AI-based tools, and attitudes toward the technology’s societal implications. The findings show a persistent gap between exposure to AI and perceived understanding of it: despite growing media visibility and public discussion, most Italians still report low levels of information. At the same time, the use of AI-based tools increased markedly between 2023 and 2024, especially in relation to chatbots and other generative applications. Public attitudes are strongly context-dependent: AI is widely accepted in safety-related domains, but encounters greater resistance in areas such as journalism, education, and the workplace. Symbolic representations of AI, such as humanoid robots, also remain salient, particularly among respondents with less direct familiarity with AI applications. Multivariate analyses further show that age, education, gender, self-perceived knowledge, and practical engagement with AI significantly shape how the technology is imagined and evaluated. Overall, the Italian case reveals a pattern of critical ambivalence rather than simple technophobia, in which expectations of usefulness coexist with concerns about risks and regulation. The paper argues that understanding how different publics engage with AI is essential for developing communication and governance strategies that are socially responsive and attentive to differentiated experiences, imaginaries, and concerns.

latest.title: From swipes to intimacy: dating app adoption and offline hookup intention among male rural migrant workers
latest.abstract: Drawing on the uses and gratifications theory and social learning theory, this study establishes a convergence model to examine the predictors of dating app adoption and subsequent offline hookup intentions among male rural migrant workers in China. Theoretically, we conceptualize adoption as a mechanism where internal drives, grounded in technological affordances of portability and locationality, converge with external peer validation to shape intention. Our time-lagged survey data from 414 rural migrant workers (further validated by a supplementary sample of 326 married workers) in China confirmed that three basic user motives (pastime, distraction, and socializing), perceived social approval, and social comparison are associated with dating app adoption (DAA), with these relationships positively moderated by person-group value fit. Moreover, DAA mediates the relationship between these antecedents and offline hookup intention, with the transition significantly weakened by situational ethical misgivings. This study contributes to the literature by elucidating the moral proximity paradox in the context of economically underprivileged users, offering practical recommendations for peer-led safety interventions, employer-sponsored offline recreation, and trust-centric app design features.

latest.title: Drivers of professional and private personalization: investigating political actors, social media platforms, and their interplay
latest.abstract: Personalization is an important communication strategy of political actors on social media as it can help to engage voters. Although previous studies have enhanced our understanding about political personalization, we lack research on how different political actors and social media platforms, and their interplay, affect personalization strategies. In this study, we investigate how posts from top candidate and political party accounts affect professional and private personalization as well as how these effects are moderated by Facebook and Instagram as platforms. To do so, we conducted a quantitative content analysis of N = 2,028 posts in the last four weeks of the 2024 Austrian National Council campaign. Using binary logistic regression with mixed effects, we find that posts from top candidate accounts are more likely than those from political party accounts to include private personalization, but do not differ in terms of professional personalization. These effects were not moderated by Facebook and Instagram as platforms. Our findings demonstrate that the actor type rather than the platform influences personalization strategies. The absence of platform-specific differences for both professional and private personalization points more toward platform convergence rather than divergence.

latest.title: Fixing election interference, safeguarding election integrity? Developments and dynamics of election-related policies on social media platforms
latest.abstract: Platforms are key intermediaries of public and political communication, both heralded as facilitators of bottom-up democracy and condemned as democracy’s greatest danger. From misinformation to hate speech to election integrity concerns, the perils of platforms have become obvious in recent years, and platforms have increasingly developed rules and processes to handle problematic content. Elections are a catalyst for this development as both moments of peak attention on platforms’ roles in democracy and of vulnerability to political interference. In this paper, we identify and compare election-related policies on key social media platforms (YouTube, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter/X, and TikTok), and examine their changes over time. We identify an early phase addressing threats to concrete election-related processes and persons (2018–2020), a much more political phase taking their roles as hosts of public conversation seriously and affirming responsibility for the integrity of civic processes (2020–2022), and a more recent phase of profound backlash (since 2022). Contextualizing these phases, we assume that general dynamics in discourses about the responsibility of platforms, as well as specific election-related developments, most notably US elections 2016–2024, explain these changes.

latest.title: Latent communicative figurations: mapping quasi-visible strategic relational structures on Facebook
latest.abstract: This study conceptualises latent communicative figurations, which are quasi-visible relational structures formed through social media affordances, for example as provided by partnership advertisement systems. We argue that latent communicative figurations are facilitated by platform affordances that enable the curation of visibility, allowing actors to form latent ties for mobilising partners to create and publish social media content that serve specific strategic interests. A systematic approach is proposed to map the positionality of two types of actors – partners (investors) and pages – who contribute to latent communicative figurations, situated between platform designers and the broader networked publics. A sample of branded Facebook posts related to renewable energy is used to construct four bi-partite networks, revealing the structure of latent relations and dominant actors within them. The results show the emergence of a primarily organisational and professional set of latent ties, which mobilises public reactions surrounding renewable energy. The results evidence a dual process of deinstitutionalisation and reinstitutionalisation where actors such as news media transition from their conventional roles to those that are demanded by profit-driven platform logics. The tensions inherent in this transition – where actors must balance the expectations of strategic partners against the public interest – reveal the fundamental antagonisms within networked social environments.

latest.title: Reddit users’ reactance to the 2025 CDC Data Purge: Characterizing the removal of health information as a perceived threat to individual freedom
latest.abstract: Following an executive order signed by Donald Trump to prevent ‘woke ideology’ from permeating everyday American lives and institutions, the Department of Health and Human Services complied by removing a large amount of health-related information from government websites. These information pages and websites pertain to reproductive health, adolescent and LGBTQ + health, and HIV. In response, contributors to the subreddit r/DataHoarder collaboratively moved to archive and preserve as much of this health information as possible. Informed by psychological reactance theory (PRT), we examine how contributors to the r/DataHoarder subreddit (a) characterize the 2025 CDC Data Purge as a perceived threat to their freedom(s) and articulate motivations to regain such freedom(s), as well as (b) describe their efforts to archive data as a means of restoration. Employing reflexive thematic analysis, we identified four major themes: Defining the Data Purge: ‘A Modern book banning’; Act now! Motivation (or lack thereof) to archive CDC data; Restoration in the context of the 2025 CDC Data Purge; and Bounding the group: r/DataHoarder camaraderie. We conclude by discussing the significance of this politically-driven discourse in a mediated context, theoretical implications for PRT, and future avenues for research.

latest.title: The viral gender antagonism on social media: examining the role of multimodal framing and gender identity
latest.abstract: What drives viral gender-antagonistic discourse on social media? This study proposes to examine the role of multimodal framing and gender identity cues. We analyzed 22,925 posts and 1.15 million comments related to sexual violence on Weibo, one of the most prominent social media platforms in China. Results from generalized linear mixed models show that multimodal framing strategies including sensationalizing and personalizing framing significantly increase gender antagonism, particularly when the message is posted by someone of the outgroup gender. In contrast, entertaining framing reduces gender antagonism, while explanatory framing has a neutral effect. Gender dynamics also play a critical role: female commenters are more reactive to male-authored sensationalizing posts. These results highlight the importance of framing strategies and identity perceptions in shaping discourse on gender issues, offering insights for social media governance and feminist communication practices.

latest.title: Mediated information grounds: living with(in) pareshani , social networks and gendered media practices among the Rohingya refugees
latest.abstract: The rapid expansion of information and communication technologies (ICTs) and social media has fundamentally transformed the production, distribution, and consumption of information, especially within marginalised and displaced communities. Drawing on qualitative data, this study investigates the information practices of Rohingya refugees and their navigation of environments shaped by genocide and prolonged displacement. The findings indicate that trauma, persistent uncertainty, and insecurity generate pareshani (anxiety), which significantly shapes media use and information behaviour. In response, refugees develop collaborative strategies to build social networks that resist exploitation, surveillance, and misinformation. These practices are situated within gendered, transnational, and socio-digital dynamics that traverse both geographical and digital boundaries. The study introduces the concept of ‘Mediated Information Grounds’ to illustrate the interplay among space, trust, privacy, and community engagement across diverse contexts. This framework demonstrates how ICT-mediated information practices intersect with technical, relational, and spatial dimensions, enabling individuals to co-create meaning, negotiate identity, and foster resilience. Overall, the study provides a nuanced account of how marginalised populations construct hybrid information ecosystems grounded in networked, participatory communication, thereby contributing to scholarship on information and communication practices in complex and precarious environments.

latest.title: Engineering infrastructural power over software production: the case of software-as-a-service
latest.abstract: Over the past two decades, vendors have moved the development, operation and maintenance of enterprise software into cloud infrastructures managed by a handful of cloud companies. Critical scholars have recognized this capacity to produce and deliver software at scale – now often referred to as software-as-a-service, or SaaS – as part of cloud companies’ growing infrastructural power. However, while prior scholarship has examined the political economic ramifications of this entanglement, it often treats scalability and infrastructural power as accomplished facts, rather than contested concepts.This article complicates these concepts by examining the emergence of SaaS at a time when neither the scalability nor the infrastructural power of cloud companies was yet stabilized. Drawing on diverse sources, it analyzes Salesforce as a case that provides insight into how incremental discursive and material efforts at consolidating its infrastructural power over software production shaped the conditions under which the deployment of scalable software services to a vast number of client organizations became possible. By foregrounding software production, this article treats scalability as a sociotechnical achievement forged alongside ongoing attempts by cloud companies to establish and defend their infrastructural power, rather than an inherent attribute of contemporary cloud infrastructures. In doing so, it contributes to critical scholarship on cloud computing by underlining the co-constitutive nature of infrastructural power and scalability while situating them as fragile – rather than firmly established and uncontested – outcomes of historical contingencies.

latest.title: Mistrust as a precondition for critical thinking and media literacy
latest.abstract: Media literacy can help individuals identify misinformation, including content that is deliberately and falsely presented as news. A key yet underexplored component of media literacy is how mistrust acts as a precondition for a critical disposition towards information sources and the claims they make. This study introduces the concept of mistrust within the context of verifying information and explores its relationship to media literacy. We conducted two interlinked online surveys (n = 2,115). The first measured participants’ confidence in their ability to verify information, as well as their experiences with media literacy education. The second survey assessed their actual ability to identify misinformation through a performance-based verification task involving four posts and articles sourced from social media and websites. Our findings indicate that both mistrust and news consumption are associated with participants’ confidence and ability to verify information. However, we observed nuanced differences between perceived confidence and actual verification ability. Mistrust emerged as the strongest predictor of confidence in identifying facts and verifying information. In contrast, actual ability was most strongly linked to online news consumption—regular news consumers were more adept at discerning misinformation. The impact of media literacy education was nuanced. Online media literacy education was positively associated with both confidence and ability, whereas school-based media literacy education primarily boosted confidence. Support from community-based organisations or family and friends, however, showed no significant relationship with either confidence or ability.

latest.title: Older adults’ perceptions, needs, and uses of social media and messenger apps as sources of information and news: a qualitative multi-method study
From the room to the screen: how video conferencing reshapes gendered interpersonal behaviors
latest.abstract: Amidst debates about remote work and the return to office, less is known about how video conferencing reshapes gender differences in interpersonal behaviors, potentially mitigating or reproducing gender inequality. This study explores how individuals experience gendered interpersonal behaviors in video conferencing and identifies which of its features reshape these behaviors. Based on 26 interviews with professionals working in small-to-medium workgroups, the findings suggest that video conferencing can mitigate gender disparities in interpersonal behaviors. The absence of physical copresence and limited visual information can enhance women’s participation by reducing gender performativity and status cues. Additionally, digital tools like virtual hand-raising and technological constraints (e.g., limited voice overlap) foster turn-taking norms, promoting equal participation and reducing interruptions. However, potential drawbacks include enhanced visual bias, limited social feedback, and the adverse impact of mirrored self-view, which may decrease women’s participation. Contrary to previous research, close-distance eye gaze does not appear to contribute to gendered interpersonal behaviors. This study highlights how gendered interpersonal behaviors are shaped by both cultural beliefs and the structural affordances of virtual environments, offering both opportunities and challenges for greater gender equity.

latest.title: Calling out disclosures, protecting followers: the new governors of influencer culture on TikTok
Evaluating metrics of fairness: a critical analysis of AI in hiring practices
latest.abstract: AI-mediated hiring is increasingly recognized as a high-stakes domain under emerging global regulatory frameworks, prompting new questions about how notions of fairness and suitability are constructed and communicated. Drawing on research in algorithmic opacity and quantification, this study critically examines how AI hiring tools frame these concepts discursively. Through an analysis of technical documents, marketing materials, and public narratives, we examine how two major hiring platforms – LinkedIn Recruiter and HireVue – frame and communicate ideas of fairness and suitability. We identify three paradoxes central to AI-mediated hiring: the discrepancy between claimed algorithmic fairness and potential embedded biases, the tension between efficiency and human discretion, and the challenges of cultural inclusivity in globally marketed tools. We treat these materials as relational artifacts that mediate values, expectations, and accountabilities among platform vendors, employers, and job seekers. While these platforms aim to mitigate bias, they reveal deeper tensions around transparency, accountability, and the normative assumptions underpinning the evolving landscape of AI-mediated recruitment.
